deep.reconstruction:
The page holds four separate research notes (programme items). Judging from the Hoppe 1893–94 reference on the next page, they date to the mid-1890s.

(1) End of a note begun on p.22: continuity in the language of Cantor fundamental sequences. Setting: an irrational number a is given by a fundamental (Cauchy) sequence (a_1, a_2, …), and one considers all fundamental sequences defining the same a. Let f be a real function.
Claim: f is continuous at x = a iff, for every fundamental sequence (a_n) representing a, the sequence (f(a_1), f(a_2), …) is again fundamental.
Further claim, said to be 'easy to show': all these image sequences then represent one and the same number, and that number is f(a).
Modern form: f is continuous at a iff for every sequence a_n → a, (f(a_n)) is Cauchy. Then lim f(a_n) is independent of the sequence and equals f(a).
[Implicit steps, mine]
- Uniqueness of the limit: given two admissible sequences (a_n) and (a'_n), interleave them as (a_1, a'_1, a_2, a'_2, …). This also converges to a, so its image is Cauchy, which forces lim f(a_n) = lim f(a'_n).
- Equality with f(a): requires an admissible sequence that hits a, e.g. the constant sequence (a, a, …).
- Necessity: continuity implies f(a_n) → f(a), hence the image is Cauchy.
The author's corrections show the drafting: 'eine Fundamentalreihe ist' became 'sämmtlich Fundamentalreihen sind', and 'und wenn' was struck.

(2) Question: which algebraic numbers 'satisfy' linear differential equations of first and second order, in the author's own sense 'determined by congruences'? The congruence-defined notion is not explained on the page. It plausibly transfers the theory of algebraic functions satisfying linear ODEs (Fuchs, Schwarz) to algebraic numbers, with derivatives or equations interpreted modulo primes.
Second-order idea: check whether the quotient of two integrals (solutions), η = y_1/y_2, can be inverted, as in Schwarz's theory, where inverting a hypergeometric period ratio gives the modular function λ(τ) or j(τ). Such an inverse function would then produce the values of elliptic functions at singular moduli: the algebraic numbers of complex multiplication, e.g. j(i) = 1728 and j((1+√−163)/2) = −640320^3. This is a heuristic research programme with no derivation.

(3) Riemann's contour integral
ζ(s) = Γ(1−s)/(2πi) ∮ (−x)^{s−1}/(e^x − 1) dx
gives at negative integers ζ(−n) = (−1)^n B_{n+1}/(n+1). Equivalently ζ(2n) = (−1)^{n+1} (2π)^{2n} B_{2n} / (2(2n)!), with the B_k the Taylor coefficients of x/(e^x − 1).
The proposal is to derive the rationality of the Bernoulli numbers from this integral representation. The hope is to get a better estimate for 'the value of the largest number contained in it', most plausibly the largest prime dividing the numerator.
This connects to Kummer's regularity criterion (p regular iff p divides no numerator of B_2, …, B_{p−3}) and to the irregular-determinant problem on the previous page. No computation is carried out.

(4) 'Prove Wiener's assertion' (H. Wiener, Halle 1891, Jahresbericht/Verhandlungen p. 8). Continued on the next page, it reads: the special Pascal theorem (Pappus) cannot be derived from the theorem on perspective triangles (Desargues). Moreover, plane Desargues cannot be proved without using space when only incidence ('existence') axioms are used, not order/continuity ('Lagen') axioms. This is a programme statement only.
errors: Item (1), sufficiency: in the setting of the previous page, fundamental sequences consist of rationals and a is irrational. On that reading the condition 'all f(a_n) are fundamental' only gives the existence of lim f(q) as q → a through the rationals. It neither forces that limit to equal f(a) nor controls f at nearby irrationals. Counterexample: f = 0 on Q and at a, f = 1 at all other irrationals. Then every image sequence is the zero sequence (value 0 = f(a)), yet f is discontinuous at a. Another: f = indicator of {a}; images are all 0, but f(a) = 1.

Item (1): the claim holds only if the admissible sequences are arbitrary real sequences converging to a, including the constant sequence a. The constant sequence is needed for the common value to equal f(a).

Item (3): rationality of Bernoulli numbers is immediate from the generating function x/(e^x − 1). Riemann's integral adds nothing to rationality itself. The goal ('the largest number contained in it') is vague; whether a numerator-prime bound could follow this way is unjustified speculation.
Items (2) and (4) are programmes, not derivations, so there are no computational errors to check.

results.what: Continuity at a point characterized by images of Cauchy (fundamental) sequences being Cauchy, with a common limit equal to f(a)
results.modern_name: Sequential (Heine) characterization of continuity / Cauchy criterion

results.what: Programme: algebraic numbers 'satisfying' linear ODEs of order 1, 2 in a congruence-defined sense; inverting the quotient of solutions of a 2nd-order ODE to obtain values of elliptic functions at singular moduli
results.modern_name: Schwarz/Fuchs inversion of period ratios (modular functions), complex multiplication / singular moduli; loosely foreshadows arithmetic (p-adic) differential equations
results.usually_credited_to: Schwarz (1873), Kronecker/Weber (CM); arithmetic differential equations: Dwork, Buium (much later)

results.what: Derive rationality of Bernoulli numbers from Riemann's contour integral for ζ, aiming at estimates for their prime factors
results.modern_name: ζ(−n) = (−1)^n B_{n+1}/(n+1); Kummer's criterion for irregular primes

results.what: Prove Wiener's claims: Pappus not derivable from Desargues; plane Desargues not provable from plane incidence axioms alone
results.modern_name: Independence results of Grundlagen der Geometrie: non-Desarguesian planes, non-Pappian (non-commutative) planes
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert (1899), building on Wiener (1891); Hessenberg (1905) for Pappus ⇒ Desargues

deep.surprise_reason: Most of the content is routine (sequential continuity, Bernoulli/ζ) or already famously Hilbert's (the Wiener-inspired Desargues/Pappus programme leading to the Grundlagen). The mildly notable item is the private idea of a 'congruence-defined' sense in which algebraic numbers satisfy linear differential equations, tied to singular moduli. It shows early Hilbert thinking along Kronecker-Jugendtraum and number-field/function-field analogy lines, but it is only a vague question.

checkable.asserts: Values of ζ at negative integers are rational, given by Bernoulli numbers (consequence of Riemann's integral); expect zeros
Euler's formula for ζ(2n) via Bernoulli numbers (n=3 instance); expect 0
Bernoulli numbers are rational Taylor coefficients of x/(e^x−1)
Numerator of B_12 is −691; the prime 691 is irregular (Kummer), the kind of 'largest contained number' at issue
von Staudt–Clausen: denominator of B_12 is 2730
j(i) = 1728: value of the inverted period ratio at a singular modulus (algebraic, here rational)
j((1+√−163)/2) = −640320^3, an integer singular modulus value; expect ≈ 0

transcription_corrections: Line 2: the image reads '(f(a_1), f(a_2), …)'; the transcription drops the closing parenthesis after a_1.
Line 3: 'sämmtlich' is written above the struck-out 'eine', and 'sind' above the struck-out 'ist'.
Line 3–4: the struck-out 'solches' corrected to 'solche' is consistent with the image.
Item (2): 'In meinem[?]' fits the image ('In meinem', with a hyphen-like stroke at the line end); the reading 'In meinem, d.h. durch Congruenzen bestimmten Sinne' is accepted.
Item (3): 'Bernullischen' is Hilbert's own spelling (sic, for Bernoullischen). 'in ihr[?]' is uncertain; it could be 'in ihr' or 'in ihnen'.
Item (4): 'Beweise die Wienersche Behauptung, (Verhandlungen …) S. 8,' — the image shows 'S. 8,)', i.e. a comma-parenthesis; the specific theorem is 'der specielle Pascalsche Satz'.
